content: Training is essential for healthcare providers already delivering care, and palliative care must be incorporated into the education of health workers and allied health professionals. Palliative care is most effectively delivered by a multidisciplinary team. Providers at all levels, from palliative care specialists to trained volunteers, collaborate to ensure the highest quality of life for patients. In tertiary care settings, the team may include an oncologist, internal medicine physician, radiotherapist, radiotherapy technician, psychologist or counselor, nutritionist, physiotherapist, oncology nurse, pharmacist, social worker, and palliative care nurse. In resource-limited settings, community health workers or trained volunteers, supported and supervised by primary and secondary healthcare professionals, are the primary providers of palliative care. Trained community nurses, such as auxiliary nurses or palliative nursing aides, can play a significant role in care delivery if permitted within the system. Family members also play a critical role in home-based care and require adequate support. Primary and community care are vital for providing palliative care services to the majority of people in need. Much of the care for dying individuals must occur in the community and across all healthcare settings, primarily managed by generalist healthcare professionals rather than specialists. Most individuals with advanced chronic conditions requiring palliative care live in the community, and with appropriate training, primary care professionals should be able to identify them. Palliative care services require expertise in managing disease complications, pain, and other symptoms, as well as providing psychosocial support to patients and families. Care for the dying and bereaved is also a critical component. Additionally, palliative care teams must possess skills in communication, decision-making, and spiritual understanding. Understanding these roles and responsibilities enables palliative care teams to function effectively and informs training needs. Community health workers and palliative nursing aides should coordinate their activities with caregivers at primary and secondary levels. Their tasks include developing individualized home-based care plans, providing treatments, instructing families, facilitating access to supplies and medications, conducting regular home visits, reporting problems to higher levels, and training patients and families in care procedures. They also assess patients' physical, psychosocial, and spiritual needs and ensure the availability of treatments, including pain management. Staff nurses at primary, secondary, and tertiary care facilities have supervisory, coordination, and teaching roles. They oversee home care, liaise between community care systems and higher-level institutions, and provide specialized nursing procedures such as lymphedema and stoma care. They also ensure proper documentation of home care. Physicians and authorized prescribers at primary and secondary care facilities manage severe symptoms, prescribe medications, and train and advise staff, patients, and families. They may visit communities to train home-based care workers, participate in palliative care training, supervise community teams, and provide treatments such as oral morphine for pain management. They also educate patients and families on preventing and managing common problems like contractures and bedsores, refer patients to higher facilities for acute issues, and provide short-term inpatient care for severe symptom management. Providers at tertiary care levels, including hospitals, deliver inpatient care for patients with intractable pain and other symptoms, including radiotherapy and other treatments available only at this level. They also provide outpatient emergency care for distressing symptoms, maintain patients as pain-free as possible using appropriate opioid dosages, and consult with referring providers. Families play an essential role in palliative care. Healthcare workers must ensure that patients and their families understand the nature and prognosis of the disease and the recommended treatments. Families also have their own needs for support, health, and social care. With the help of healthcare workers, families are involved in joint decision-making, kept informed of medical decisions, and guided in best practices for palliative care. Families and other caregivers can be taught to provide home-based care. Task-shifting is a strategy to use the available health workforce cost-effectively while expanding palliative care services to the community. Certain palliative care activities can be transferred from specialized doctors to other healthcare professionals. For example, in Uganda, nurses and clinical officers who complete a nine-month palliative care course are authorized to prescribe morphine. This course includes theoretical training, practical placements, and implementation planning for palliative care services. Graduates are expected to lead palliative care coordination in their districts, organize case conferences, and advocate for integrating palliative care into district and community plans. Strengthening palliative care in the primary care workforce involves training all healthcare workers in the target area, including community leaders and family caregivers, in basic home-based care. Education should be synchronized with the introduction of new services, such as making oral morphine and other essential medications available. In-service training in the target area can help healthcare providers remain connected to their working environment while contributing to the organization and implementation of palliative care services.
